headline: The week the Treasury market stopped waiting for the Fed
standfirst: Weekend edition. The ten-year yield went from 4.95% on Monday to 5.21% on Thursday, its highest since 2007; the thirty-year to 5.49%, its highest since 2004; and every Treasury from two years out now yields five or more. It took a flash PMI at a five-year high, three coupon auctions that each cleared at a two-decade high with a little less demand than the last, and eight Fed officials — five of them voters — saying some version of “more” while the Chair said nothing. October is 71% priced; swaps carry three hikes over the next year. Equities absorbed it: the S&P 500 is up 0.7% on the week at 7,704.13 and the Nasdaq 1.6% after two record closes, while the Dow is down 0.6% for a fourth losing week and utilities lost 4.2%. Brent round-tripped from $100 to $99 to $106 on Iran. Friday brings durable goods and Michigan; the week ahead brings the RBA, PCE, quarter-end, Micron and September payrolls.

bullets.title: Three auctions, three two-decade highs, and a buyback that could not fill
bullets.text: Treasury sold $69 billion of two-years at 4.787% on Tuesday (the highest since May 2024, demand average), $70 billion of five-years at 5.033% on Wednesday (the highest since June 2006, 3bp cheap, dealers left with the most paper since 2024) and $44 billion of seven-years at 5.085% on Thursday (the highest since the tenor was reintroduced in 2009, 0.7bp cheap, indirect bidders at 57.2%, the least since November 2025). Between the second and third, Treasury's buyback of 20- to 30-year bonds accepted $4.1 billion of a $6 billion cap — 68% against 86% a fortnight earlier — and thirty-year municipal yields went through 5% for the first time since 2011. The MOVE index closed Wednesday at its highest since March. Mortgage rates are back above 7% for the first time since May 2024, and Stifel's note put total federal debt above $40 trillion. The next coupon supply is the ten-year on 7 October and the thirty-year on 8 October.

bullets.title: Why: a 58.4 PMI, and a Fed that has stopped arguing with itself
bullets.text: Wednesday's flash composite PMI printed 58.4 against 55.3 expected, the highest since July 2021, with services at 58.7, manufacturing at 57.0 and the input-price index at 66.4, the highest since October 2022; S&P Global's Chris Williamson put it at about 5% annualised growth. Then the speakers: Governor Barr on Wednesday said further hikes are “likely needed” and the Fed had been “out of position”; on Thursday Williams said another hike this year is “reasonable” and that the era of forward guidance is over, Paulson — who had favoured holding in September — said “some modest further tightening may be warranted”, and Hammack said the longer inflation persists the costlier it is to remove. Barkin, Collins, Goolsbee and Musalem said the same earlier in the week. Chair Warsh has said nothing between meetings, by design. October went from 49% a week ago to 71%; December is about 94%; CME futures imply as many as four more quarter-points by the end of 2027. Thursday's data agreed: claims 197,000, new home sales 684,000 against 620,000, Kansas City Fed 20 against 17.

bullets.title: Oil: a $7 round trip on tankers, talks and a Houthi strike
bullets.text: Brent settled at $100.34 on Monday, $99.25 on Tuesday — its first close under $100 since 9 September, on Saudi pipeline tests and a three-hour US–Iran meeting — then $103.08 on Wednesday and $106.41 on Thursday, up 3.2% on the day and the highest close since 15 September. The reversal was Iran's president telling the UN the country would not surrender, a cargo vessel struck inside Hormuz, Houthi missile and drone attacks on Riyadh and Aramco's Yanbu facilities, and Iran's military saying it could widen the war to the Indian Ocean. Against that, Reuters reported US and Iranian negotiators exploring a phased path — Tehran reopens the strait, Washington lifts the port blockade — and the S&P 500 came off its lows on it. Trump floated and then walked back a diesel export ban within a day. Brent is up 17.6% in September and 75% on the year; WTI shows a 6.4% weekly fall only because its front month rolled to November. Overnight both are lower, Brent near $105.7.

bullets.title: Equities held, narrowly, on Meta and AMD
bullets.text: The Nasdaq set records on Monday and Tuesday, fell 1.13% on Wednesday and closed Thursday flat at 26,939.37, up 1.6% on the week; the S&P 500 is 0.7% higher at 7,704.13; the Dow is 0.6% lower at 51,349.98, a fourth straight weekly loss and a three-month low; the Russell 2000 is off 0.9%. The leadership was narrow: Meta rose 11.43% on Monday when its Muse agent topped the App Store and 4.5% on Thursday to $777.59, more than 30% on the month; AMD closed above a $1 trillion valuation on Monday and then gave back. On Monday more S&P 500 stocks set 52-week lows than highs, the first time that has happened on a record day since December 1999. Financials lost 2.38% on the week and utilities 4.23%; Oracle fell 3.5% on Thursday after a force majeure notice on a New Mexico data centre, with its credit-default swaps at a record. After the bell, Akamai rose about 20% on an $11.6 billion seven-year deal with Anthropic and Costco beat. FactSet has third-quarter S&P 500 earnings growing about 29%; the banks open the season on 13 October.

bullets.title: The week ahead: RBA Monday, PCE and quarter-end Wednesday, payrolls Friday
bullets.text: Xi Jinping left Washington with the trade truce extended to 10 January and nothing else — the summit produced warm words, no movement on Taiwan, Iran or AI, and Trump saying “let’s leave AI as it is” against Xi’s “under human control”. Monday the RBA decides with about 90% priced for a hike from 4.35% after August jobs printed +39,500. Tuesday: JOLTS, consumer confidence, and Musalem, Goolsbee and Williams. Wednesday is quarter-end and the week's heaviest day: ADP (previous 38,000), August PCE with core at 3.3% year on year last month, final Q2 GDP at 1.5%, Chicago PMI, China's PMIs, Australian CPI, German CPI, UK GDP, Micron after the close and Kashkari after that. Thursday: ISM manufacturing (previous 54.6, prices paid 71.1), Challenger, claims, Nike, and Chinese markets shut for Golden Week through 7 October. Friday 2 October: September payrolls after August's 162,000, unemployment at 4.1%, hourly earnings at 3.1%, and the euro-area flash HICP against 3.2%. The FOMC minutes follow on 7 October, the ten- and thirty-year auctions on 7 and 8, and JPMorgan, Goldman, Wells Fargo and Citi on the 13th.

calendar.note: Williams for a second day. He said Thursday that forward guidance is over and another hike this year is reasonable; a repeat would be the message.
Seen −0.4% after +1.1%, ex-transport +0.6%, core capital goods +0.5% off a July revised to flat. After a 57.0 manufacturing PMI, the risk is to the upside.
Seen 47.6 after 47.8. The one-year inflation expectation at 4.6% is the line the Fed reads; Michigan's household number and the Fed's own 2.4% business number are two points apart.
About 90% priced for a hike from 4.35% after +39,500 jobs against 20,000 expected. Bullock has said she is not signalling the path; the market has signalled it for her.
Openings were 7.27 million. Fed speakers around it: Musalem 07:30, Goolsbee 13:00, Williams 14:00 ET.

calendar.event: PCE (August); final Q2 GDP; ADP 08:15; quarter-end
calendar.note: Core PCE was 3.3% year on year and 0.2% on the month; headline 3.7%. The print the Fed named. Micron reports after the close, Kashkari speaks at 18:00 ET, and quarter-end flows sit on top of all of it.

calendar.event: ISM manufacturing (September); Nike after the close
calendar.note: Previous 54.6 with prices paid at 71.1. The flash PMI said 57.0 with input prices at a four-year high; a matching ISM would confirm the repricing. China is shut for Golden Week from today.

August was 162,000 with unemployment 4.1% and hourly earnings 3.1%. With October at 71%, a strong print does not add a hike so much as remove the last doubt; a weak one is the only thing on the calendar that could take it away.

sessionNote: Friday's tape opens softer: Brent is $105.73, down 0.8%, and WTI $93.05, down 1.7%, after Thursday's rally; the dollar index is 101.2 after its first back-to-back weekly gain since June; gold is $4,301 and down 2.8% on the week; Bitcoin is $84,271. Tokyo rose 1.26%, Hong Kong fell 1.55%, Seoul is shut for Chuseok and Shanghai for Mid-Autumn. The session itself is light — durable goods at 08:30 ET, Michigan at 10:00, Williams before the open and Hammack after lunch — which is what makes it dangerous: the bond market has repriced 26bp in four sessions into no supply and a holiday-thinned Asia, and a quiet Friday is when positions get squared. The clean window is the US morning. Anything after 14:00 ET is a weekend headline being priced by whoever is left.
watchOut: Assuming the bond market is finished. The ten-year rose 26bp in four sessions on a survey, three auctions and speeches; next week has no coupon supply, which sounds like relief, but it also has PCE, quarter-end rebalancing out of the asset class that fell least into the one that fell most, and a payrolls print that only matters if it is weak. A market that demanded 5.085% for seven-year paper on Thursday has not said what it wants for ten-year paper on 7 October. The second trap is the one that has held all month: trading oil on the last headline. Brent moved $7 in three days on a pipeline test, a meeting, a speech and a missile; the phased-deal report that lifted stocks on Thursday came from the same wire that reported the Houthi strike. Size for the range, not the direction.

archive.headline: A survey took the ten-year to 5.11%. An auction kept it there.
archive.summary: A flash composite PMI of 58.4, the highest since July 2021, took the ten-year up 14.6bp to 5.116% — its worst day since April 2025 — and a $70 billion five-year auction stopped at 5.033%, the highest since 2006. Barr said further hikes were likely needed and October went to 73% priced; every sector but energy fell and Brent rose back above $100.

archive.headline: The Fed said “we’ll see”. The two-year auction said 4.787%.
archive.summary: Treasury sold $69 billion of two-years at 4.787%, the highest stop since May 2024, on demand that held; Brent settled at $99.25 for its first close under $100 since 9 September; four Fed officials, none voting this year, all leaned toward more. The Nasdaq closed at a second straight record while financials fell 1.97%.

archive.headline: An App Store ranking moved a trillion dollars
archive.summary: Meta's Muse agent topped the US iPhone chart and the CPU complex repriced around it: Meta +11.43%, AMD +9.95% to a first $1 trillion close, Intel +12%, Arm +17%, and the Nasdaq to its first record since June. Crude fell to an eleven-day low on Hormuz shipping data and the ten-year came back under 5%, into a $69 billion two-year auction.

archive.headline: The war premium leaks out before the UN
archive.summary: Monday with no US data and a live diplomatic wire. Crude fell for a fourth session as traders priced a chance of US–Iran contact at the UN General Assembly and Saudi Arabia worked to restore its East–West pipeline, with the ten-year coming into the day at 5.01% after its first close above 5% since July 2007.

archive.headline: The hike landed. The bond market blinked first.
archive.summary: Weekend edition. The Fed's unanimous 25bp on Wednesday took the Dow down 631 points and Thursday gave most of it back, with the S&P up 1.14% to 7,637.76 as the ten-year fell to 4.93% and oil slid. The weekend risk was the Iran war, with Trump saying he was near a decision on resuming large-scale strikes.

archive.headline: The ten-year touched 5% into the decision. The hike is not the event.
archive.summary: FOMC day. The 10-year had closed at 5.00% after touching 5.04%, the highest since 2007, with a 25bp hike priced at 92–94%. WTI had jumped 5.1% to $106.56 as fighting intensified in the Middle East; every US sector but energy closed red on Tuesday.

archive.headline: Core CPI ran hot into an FOMC that is now 90% priced to hike
archive.summary: Weekend edition. Core CPI rose 0.3% on the month against 0.2% expected, PPI came in at 5.4% year-over-year, and September hike odds moved from 61% to about 90%. Equities closed the week higher regardless — S&P +0.86% Friday, VIX −11% — while the 10-year finished at 4.96%.
